t: Governor of Judah, or of the tribe of Judah?
p: The Hebrew gives Zerubbabel the Persian title. The Greek calls him of the tribe of Judah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 reads the word at 1:14
readings.en: governor of Judah
readings.plain: governor of Judah

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (also 1:14; 2:2, 21, and added at 1:12)
readings.en: from the tribe of Judah
readings.plain: of the tribe of Judah

why: The Hebrew title pechah is the Persian-period word for a provincial governor (Ezra 5:3), and Mur88 has it visibly at 1:14. The Greek avoids the title in every place the Hebrew has it, so it is probably the translator's choice (a Persian office meant little to a Greek reader), not a different Hebrew text. The Hebrew word is also in 2:21.
b: In 1:1 the scrolls are broken exactly at this word (4Q77 and Mur88 both have it only as a restoration), so they cannot be cited here. The Greek makes Zerubbabel a tribal leader, not an official of the Persian king; the Hebrew shows that the book names the empire's structure openly. The Hebrew of 1:12 has no title for Zerubbabel, so there the Greek adds the phrase. A small spelling difference: 4Q77 writes the king's name Darius as dryhsh (דריהש) at 1:1 where the Masoretic Text has dryvsh (דריוש); this is a spelling variant, not a different name.

a: The time has not come, the time for rebuilding the LORD's house
t: "Not the time, the time of the house"
p: The Hebrew repeats the word "time" in an awkward clause. The Greek says it once.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the second "time" and the end of the verse are visible)
readings.en: not the time to come, the time of the LORD's house to be rebuilt
readings.plain: The time has not come, the time for rebuilding the LORD's house

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: οὐχ ἥκει ὁ καιρὸς τοῦ οἰκοδομῆσαι τὸν οἶκον Κυρίου
readings.en: the time has not come to build the LORD's house
readings.plain: The time has not come to rebuild the LORD's house

why: The Hebrew is the harder text and Mur88 agrees with it. The Greek reads smoothly and could be a tidying of the doubled "time," or could reflect a shorter Hebrew; no Hebrew witness read here supports it. The clumsy Hebrew sounds like a quotation of an excuse.
b: The Hebrew has the infinitive bo', "to come," where a finite "has come" would be expected. 4Q77 has "not time" (lo' 'et) visibly, with the next word restored, and then breaks off.

t: "And I will be honored": written one way, read another
p: A scribal note says the word is written without its last letter, he, and read with it. The meaning is the same.

readings.w: Reading tradition (qere) and the vowels of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: and let me be honored
readings.plain: and I will be honored

readings.w: Written text (ketiv), as the Talmud and the Masoretic notation record it
readings.en: and I will be honored
readings.plain: and I will be honored

why: Both forms of the verb mean "be honored." The Plain English Translation follows the reading tradition, which is what the Leningrad Codex's vowels give. The ketiv/qere difference does not change the sense.
b: A Jewish teaching builds on the missing letter. The letter he stands for the number five, so the absent he was taken to mean that five things were missing from the Second Temple: the ark with its cover and cherubim, the fire from heaven, the Shekhinah (the divine presence), the Holy Spirit (prophecy), and the Urim and Thummim (Bavli Yoma 21b; compare the list in Yoma 9b). Rashi gives the same teaching. This is a lesson drawn from spelling, not a claim about the original meaning of the verb. The Murabba'at scroll has the word only in a restored form, so it cannot be cited. The Septuagint renders "and I will be glorified."

a: the heavens over you have held back dew
t: Over you, or because of you?
p: The Hebrew has "over (or on) you," which the Greek leaves out.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("over you" is visible)
readings.en: over you the heavens have held back from dew
readings.plain: the heavens over you have held back dew

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: the sky will hold back from dew
readings.plain: the heavens have held back dew

why: The Hebrew is supported by Mur88, and "over you" fits the covenant curse in which the sky above them stays shut (Deuteronomy 28:23). The Greek has no word for "you" and uses the future tense, so it is probably a looser rendering.
b: 'Alekhem can mean "over you" or "because of you." Either way the Hebrew puts the cause on the hearers.

p: The consonants of the Hebrew word can be read "drought" (choreb) or "sword" (chereb). The Masoretes read "drought"; the Greek reads "sword."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (vowels of the Masoretes)
readings.en: drought
readings.plain: a drought

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: a sword
readings.plain: a sword

why: The context is all about dryness and failed crops (1:6, 10-11), and "drought" echoes the "desolate" house of 1:4 and 1:9. The word "summoned" fits both, since God summons a sword elsewhere (Ezekiel 38:21). The Greek is a possible reading of unvowelled letters.
b: The Hebrew was written without vowels until the Masoretes pointed it, so the reading "drought" is their tradition. Both readings are possible; the Greek translator took the other. The Murabba'at scroll has the word restored only, so it adds nothing.

p: The Hebrew calls Haggai the LORD's messenger. The Greek says "angel of the Lord among the angels of the Lord."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (mal'ak YHWH is visible)
readings.en: the messenger of the LORD with the message of the LORD
readings.plain: the LORD's messenger

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: the angel of the Lord among the angels of the Lord
readings.plain: the angel of the Lord

why: Mal'ak is the ordinary word for a human messenger as well as for an angel, and the Hebrew's second word (mal'akut, "message") makes the human sense clear. The Greek uses the word angelos in both places and reads "in the angels" for the unusual Hebrew "in the message," which lets a reader take Haggai for a heavenly being.
b: The Greek wording lets a reader take Haggai for a heavenly being; the Hebrew gives no reason for it. I did not find a named ancient writer who read it so, and none is cited. Rashi on 1:13 reads the Hebrew as a messenger of the Omnipresent.

a: the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet
p: The Hebrew says "by the hand of Haggai," as in 1:1 and 1:3. The Murabba'at scroll seems to read "to Haggai."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: by the hand of Haggai the prophet
readings.plain: the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet

readings.w: Murabba'at scroll of the Twelve, Mur88 (early 2nd century AD) (as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook)
readings.en: to Haggai the prophet
readings.plain: the word of the LORD came to Haggai the prophet

why: Haggai uses "by the hand of" (1:1, 3; 2:1) and "to" (2:10, 20). The Masoretic reading is the main witness and keeps the book's own pattern. The scroll's "to" could be a leveling to 2:10 and 2:20, or a different habit of its scribe. The meaning is the same.
b: The Septuagint has "spoke" with "by the hand of Haggai." Mur88 is the only Hebrew manuscript read here that differs.

a: As for the word that I cut with you when you came out of Egypt, my spirit is standing among you
t: The clause the Greek does not have
p: The Hebrew opens with a phrase with no verb about the Exodus covenant. The Greek omits it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the clause is visible)
readings.orig: אֶת־הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר כָּרַתִּי אִתְּכֶם בְּצֵאתְכֶם מִמִּצְרַיִם וְרוּחִי עֹמֶדֶת בְּתוֹכְכֶם
readings.en: the word that I cut with you when you came out of Egypt, and my spirit is standing among you
readings.plain: As for the word that I cut with you when you came out of Egypt, my spirit is standing among you

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ τὸ πνεῦμά μου ἐφέστηκεν ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν
readings.en: and my spirit stands among you
readings.plain: My spirit is standing among you

why: Mur88 preserves the clause and the Greek has no known Hebrew behind its shorter text. The Hebrew phrase is hard because it lacks a verb for the object marker and lacks the word "covenant" after "cut"; the Greek may have dropped it for that reason.
b: In the Hebrew the object sign 'et introduces a phrase with no verb (compare "remember" or "I keep" supplied by translators), and "cut" without "covenant" is a short form of the usual "cut a covenant" (Exodus 24:8; Deuteronomy 5:2-3). The Vulgate, a later witness, supplies a verb, pepigi, "I covenanted." The shorter Greek is the text of Swete's edition (mainly Vaticanus); other Greek witnesses, including the Hexaplaric material and the Göttingen apparatus, were not checked.

a: The prized things of all the nations will come
t: The prized things of the nations, the Desired One, or the chosen things?
p: A singular noun with a plural verb gave rise to three readings: treasures, a person, and the chosen.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the noun chemdat is visible, the verb is restored)
readings.en: the desire of all the nations, and they will come
readings.plain: The prized things of all the nations will come

readings.w: Vulgate (Jerome, late 4th century AD)
readings.en: and the Desired of all nations will come
readings.plain: The Desired of all the nations will come

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ ἥξει τὰ ἐκλεκτὰ πάντων τῶν ἐθνῶν
readings.en: and the chosen things of all the nations will come
readings.plain: The chosen things of all the nations will come

why: The Hebrew noun means "desire" or what is desired, and the plural verb makes the best sense if the noun is collective, "the desirable things" (the nations' wealth, as the next verse and Isaiah 60:5-11 suggest). A single "Desired One" requires a singular verb, which the Hebrew does not have; the Vulgate has one. The Greek's plural noun fits the Hebrew's sense. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and the collective reading.
b: The Latin reading shaped Christian use of the verse: the Advent hymns and the antiphon "O King of the nations, and their desire" (O Rex gentium et desideratus earum) echo it, and so does Charles Wesley's "Come, Thou long-expected Jesus" ("Dear desire of every nation"). Radak, the medieval commentator, reads the nations' valuables (on 2:7), and the Targum Jonathan keeps the singular noun with a plural verb. No Rashi comment on this verse was found, and whether any Hebrew manuscript has a plural noun was not checked. See the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter. The Hebrew grammar does not forbid reading the noun as a person; it only makes it harder.

a: In this place I will give peace, the LORD of Armies declares
t: The Greek adds a sentence about peace
p: The Greek adds a promise of peace of soul to everyone who builds. No Hebrew witness read here has it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (no scroll preserves this verse)
readings.orig: וּבַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה אֶתֵּן שָׁלוֹם נְאֻם יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת
readings.en: and in this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of Armies
readings.plain: In this place I will give peace, the LORD of Armies declares

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐν τῷ τόπῳ τούτῳ δώσω εἰρήνην ... καὶ εἰρήνην ψυχῆς εἰς περιποίησιν παντὶ τῷ κτίζοντι τοῦ ἀναστῆσαι τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον
readings.en: and in this place I will give peace... and peace of soul as a possession for everyone who builds, to raise up this temple
readings.plain: In this place I will give peace, the LORD of Armies declares, and peace of soul as a possession for everyone who builds, to raise up this temple

why: The Hebrew has no extra clause in the witnesses we can check, and the longer Greek reads like an expansion that spells out what "peace" means for the builders. No scroll preserves 2:9, so the plus cannot be tested against an older Hebrew.
b: The addition spells out what "peace" means for the builders: a settled mind for those who raise the house.

a: What they offer there is unclean.
t: A long addition in the Greek
p: The Greek adds three clauses after "unclean" that echo Amos 5:10.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the verse ends with the Masoretic words)
readings.en: and what they offer there is unclean
readings.plain: What they offer there is unclean.

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ ὃς ἐὰν ἐγγίσῃ ἐκεῖ, μιανθήσεται ἕνεκεν τῶν λημμάτων αὐτῶν τῶν ὀρθρινῶν, ὀδυνηθήσονται ἀπὸ προσώπου πόνων αὐτῶν· καὶ ἐμισεῖτε ἐν πύλαις ἐλέγχοντας
readings.en: and whoever comes near there will be made unclean on account of their early gains; they will be in pain at the sight of their labors; and you hated in the gates those who reprove
readings.plain: Whoever comes near there will be made unclean because of their early gains. They will be in pain at the sight of their labors. And you hated in the gates those who reprove.

why: The Hebrew is the shorter text, and Mur88 ends the verse where the Masoretic Text does. The Greek's last clause matches the wording of Amos 5:10 about hating the one who reproves in the gate, so it looks like an interpretive expansion drawn from there.
b: The Greek expansion turns the verse into a charge of corrupt gain. No Hebrew manuscript is known to have it.

p: The Hebrew counts the vat's yield in purah. The Greek uses a different measure and a different place word.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("fifty purah" is visible)
readings.en: to draw out fifty purah
readings.plain: to draw out fifty measures

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: to draw out fifty metretai
readings.plain: to draw out fifty measures

why: Purah occurs only here and in Isaiah 63:3, where it is a winepress or trough, so "measure" in this verse is a guess from the context. Some have thought the Hebrew text is damaged here, since the pairing with the first line (twenty, ten) is not exact; nothing in the Mur88 text, which has the Hebrew words, supports a different reading. The Greek names a standard liquid measure, the metretes, and speaks of the lower vat (hypolenion) where the Hebrew has the wine vat, and its first line has barley and sata where the Hebrew has only a heap. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and the general word "measures."
b: The proportions are the point: half of the grain and two fifths of the wine (see the note at 2:16). I did not check an apparatus for proposed emendations of purah.

a: none of you turned back to me
p: The Hebrew has "and not you to me," with no verb. The Greek and Amos 4:9 supply "turn back."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and none of you [turned] to me
readings.plain: none of you turned back to me

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and you did not turn back to me
readings.plain: you did not turn back to me

why: Both readings give the same sense. The Hebrew is a shortened form of the refrain "yet you did not turn back to me" in Amos 4:6, 8, 9, 10, 11, and the Plain English Translation supplies the verb from that refrain. The Greek has no Hebrew behind it that differs.
b: The Greek names two of the three afflictions differently (aphoria, "barrenness," and anemophthoria, "wind damage," for blight and mildew); its chalaza is "hail," the same as the Hebrew. The Murabba'at scroll has most of the clause only in restored form.

p: The Greek has a different opening verb and puts the last "Take it to heart" with the question of 2:19.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 reads the same words (most are visible); 4Q80 has the end of the verse in part
readings.orig: שימו נא לבבכם מן היום הזה ומעלה … שימו לבבכם
readings.en: set your heart, from this day and upward ... set your heart
readings.plain: Take it to heart

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: ὑποτάξατε δή τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν … θέσθε ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν
readings.en: submit your hearts ... put it in your hearts
readings.plain: Set your hearts

why: The Hebrew verb is the same "set your heart" as in 2:15, and 4Q80 and Mur88 give no sign of a different Hebrew text. The Greek uses a different verb at the start (hypotaxate, "put under") and ends the verse with "put it in your hearts," which it joins to the question of 2:19 ("consider whether..."); many modern translations also join the last clause to 2:19. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew verse division, so the refrain closes the verse.
b: No scroll omits the date clause ("from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month"): Mur88 has it. I did not check an apparatus for editors who treat it as an added gloss. For the foundation, see the note at 2:18.

a: Is the seed still in the barn?
t: The seed, or the threshing floor?
p: The Hebrew asks about the seed in the barn. The Greek asks whether it will be known on the threshing floor.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4Q80 and Mur88 ("is the seed" is visible in both)
readings.en: is the seed still in the barn?
readings.plain: Is the seed still in the barn?

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: whether it will be known on the threshing floor
readings.plain: Will it be known on the threshing floor?

why: Two scrolls from the Judean Desert (4Q80, which is 4QXIIe, and Mur88) read the Masoretic Hebrew, so the Greek is a different reading or a free rendering, not an older Hebrew text we can point to.
b: The Greek also joins the final "Take it to heart" of 2:18 to this clause ("consider whether..."), and many modern translations do the same. See the note at 2:18.

p: The Hebrew has "the throne of kingdoms." The Greek has "thrones of kings."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the phrase is visible)
readings.en: the throne of kingdoms
readings.plain: the throne of kingdoms

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: thrones of kings
readings.plain: the thrones of kings

why: Mur88 reads the singular "throne" and the plural "kingdoms" as the Masoretic Text does, and the Hebrew is the harder phrase (one throne standing for all kingdoms). The Greek smooths it, and also puts the next phrase in the plural, "the power of the kings of the nations."
b: The Greek of the second half of the verse also has plural chariots and riders. The Hebrew has the singular "chariot," which Mur88 also has.
